title: Real M-Spike or Impostor? Immunofixation, Therapeutic Antibodies and Specimen Artifacts
summary: See why immunofixation is more sensitive than SPEP and names the clone, how daratumumab and other IgG1 kappa drugs forge a band that can look like residual myeloma, and how fibrinogen, hemolysis and beta-region crowding fake or hide monoclonal bands.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 47 Hit 12 (IFE more sensitive than SPEP; identifies heavy and light chain), Hit 13 (daratumumab and elotuzumab IgG1 kappa bands misread as residual disease), Hit 14 (fibrinogen and hemolysis false-positive bands), Hit 19 (small beta-region bands hidden by transferrin/C3), Exam Trap 2 (M-spike does not prove active myeloma) and Exam Trap 3 (not every band is a paraprotein). Checked against Caers 2018 (EMN), Lee 2026, Pires 2025, Radocha 2021, van de Donk 2016, Ladwig 2017 and Rade 2020 (all full text via Europe PMC). Context added from the sources: drug interference matters mainly near complete response and when the patient’s clone is also IgG kappa; isatuximab also interferes; DIRA covers daratumumab only; other pseudo-peak causes include high CRP and iodinated contrast. Not taught (pending): the reviewer’s “red band visible before staining” for hemolysis and its placement of the hemolysis band near transferrin; the alpha-2 region hiding place and the claim that bands between normal proteins may be disregarded. Jenkins 2009 (Clin Biochem Rev) was read via a page-fetch tool but did not cover these artifacts.

objectives: Compare SPEP and serum immunofixation for detecting, typing and quantifying a monoclonal protein.
Explain how therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibodies interfere with SPEP/IFE response assessment and how DIRA or mass spectrometry resolves it.
Recognise specimen-related pseudo-bands (fibrinogen, hemolysis) and beta-region masking, and choose the confirming step.

scenes.title: Three bands, one question
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) results. (1) A myeloma patient in deep remission on daratumumab shows a new faint band in the gamma region; IgG kappa on immunofixation. (2) A haemodialysis patient whose blood was drawn through a heparin-locked catheter shows a narrow band between the beta and gamma zones. (3) A patient with a normal-looking SPEP whose immunofixation shows a small IgA band in the beta region. Question token: “Paraprotein or impostor?”

cues.text: Invented scenario: a myeloma patient in deep remission on daratumumab now shows a faint IgG kappa band.
A dialysis patient bled through a heparin-locked catheter shows a sharp band between beta and gamma. A third patient has a normal-looking electrophoresis, but immunofixation finds a small IgA band.
Which of these is the patient’s own clone, and which are impostors?

scenes.title: SPEP finds it, IFE names it
scenes.altText: Two method cards. SPEP separates serum proteins into zones and quantifies a monoclonal protein (M-protein) peak; its limit of detection is about 0.5–2 g/L, and co-migrating polyclonal background limits it at low levels. Serum immunofixation (IFE) overlays antisera against IgG, IgA and IgM heavy chains and kappa and lambda light chains; its limit of detection is about 0.1–0.2 g/L, roughly 5–10 times more sensitive than SPEP, but it does not quantify. Rule token: IFE is needed at diagnosis to type the M-protein, and complete response requires a negative IFE.

cues.text: Serum protein electrophoresis separates proteins into zones and measures the size of a monoclonal peak. But it only detects about half a gram to two grams per litre, and the normal polyclonal background can hide a small peak.

Immunofixation lays antisera over the gel: anti-IgG, anti-IgA and anti-IgM for the heavy chain, anti-kappa and anti-lambda for the light chain. The band that fixes with one heavy and one light chain names the clone.
Immunofixation detects about a tenth to a fifth of a gram per litre, roughly five to ten times more sensitive than electrophoresis. But it names the protein; it does not measure it.
So immunofixation is required at diagnosis to type the protein, and a complete response requires a negative immunofixation, not just a flat electrophoresis.

props.label: Diagnosis: type by IFE · complete response: IFE negative

scenes.title: The drug that forges a spike
scenes.altText: Drug cards (from a 2026 review table): daratumumab — anti-CD38, human IgG1 kappa; isatuximab — anti-CD38, humanized IgG1 kappa; elotuzumab — anti-SLAMF7, humanized IgG1 kappa. Mechanism card: therapeutic antibodies are whole immunoglobulins, so serum IFE detects them; they usually circulate below about 2 g/L, so they matter mainly in patients near very good partial or complete response, and when the patient’s own M-protein is the same isotype (IgG kappa) they cannot be told apart and can mimic residual disease. Fix card: the daratumumab IFE reflex assay (DIRA) adds an anti-daratumumab antibody that shifts the drug’s migration away from the patient’s M-protein; it works only for daratumumab; mass spectrometry can distinguish several drugs.

cues.text: Modern myeloma therapy includes monoclonal antibodies: daratumumab and isatuximab against CD38, and elotuzumab against SLAMF7. All three are IgG1 kappa molecules.

They are whole immunoglobulins, so immunofixation sees them as a monoclonal IgG kappa band. Levels are usually below about two grams per litre, so the problem appears when the patient is close to complete response.
If the patient’s own clone is also IgG kappa, the drug band and the clone cannot be told apart, and the drug can look like residual disease.
The daratumumab reflex assay adds an anti-daratumumab antibody that shifts the drug band away from the patient’s protein. It works only for daratumumab; mass spectrometry can separate several drugs.

lines: Same IgG κ clone: mimics disease

scenes.title: Tube impostors and hiding places
scenes.altText: Impostor cards. Fibrinogen: incomplete clotting (for example residual heparin from a central venous catheter) leaves fibrinogen in serum, giving a band between beta and gamma that mimics a monoclonal protein; adding thrombin removed it in most samples in one study. Hemolysis and other interferences (elevated C-reactive protein, iodinated contrast, some antibiotics) can create pseudo-M-protein peaks; one review figure shows a hemolysed, fibrinogen-containing sample with alpha-zone changes and a beta-1 peak that vanished on a new collection. Hiding-place card: IgA M-proteins often migrate in the beta region, where transferrin and C3 distort the trace and beta-migrating M-proteins are hardest to quantify; clonality must be confirmed by IFE. Hook answers: (1) suspect the drug, consider DIRA; (2) suspect fibrinogen, thrombin-treat or recollect; (3) a real IgA band hidden in beta.

cues.text: Now the tube impostors. If a sample does not clot completely, for example because of heparin from a dialysis catheter, fibrinogen stays in the serum and makes a sharp band between beta and gamma. Adding thrombin removed it in most samples in one study.

Hemolysis, a high C-reactive protein and iodinated contrast can also create false peaks. In one review’s example, a hemolysed sample with fibrinogen had a beta peak that vanished on a fresh collection.
And real bands can hide. IgA proteins often run in the beta zone, where transferrin and C3 crowd the trace, so a small band is easy to miss or mismeasure. Immunofixation confirms clonality.
Back to the hook. Patient one: suspect the drug and consider the reflex assay. Patient two: suspect fibrinogen, thrombin-treat or recollect. Patient three: a real IgA clone hiding in beta.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “An IgG kappa band on IFE in a treated patient proves active myeloma” (✓ check for a therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibody such as daratumumab, isatuximab or elotuzumab); “Every sharp band is a paraprotein” (✓ fibrinogen from incomplete clotting and hemolysis make pseudo-peaks; confirm with IFE and a good specimen); “A normal SPEP rules out an M-protein” (✓ IFE is about 5–10 times more sensitive, and beta-region bands hide behind transferrin and C3).

cues.text: Trap one: an IgG kappa band in a treated patient proves the myeloma is active. No: check the drug list for a therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibody first.
Trap two: every sharp band is a paraprotein. No: fibrinogen from an incompletely clotted sample and hemolysis make false peaks. Confirm with immunofixation and a good specimen.
Trap three: a normal electrophoresis rules out a monoclonal protein. No: immunofixation is far more sensitive, and beta bands can hide.

props.title: ✗ “IgG κ band on therapy = active myeloma.”
✗ “Normal SPEP = no M-protein.”
lines: ✓ IFE ~5–10× more sensitive; β bands hide

scenes.title: ID, tube, drug
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Before you call a band a clone, check its ID, the tube and the drug list: IFE gives the ID (heavy and light chain), the tube tells you if it clotted and is free of hemolysis, and the drug list tells you if the patient is on a therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibody.” Tokens: ID = IFE · tube = clot and hemolysis · drug = daratumumab, isatuximab, elotuzumab. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: before you call a band a clone, check its ID, the tube and the drug. Immunofixation gives the ID. The tube tells you whether it clotted and is free of hemolysis. The drug list tells you whether an IgG1 kappa antibody is on board.

Where it breaks: immunofixation cannot separate a drug from an IgG kappa clone, so the ID check alone fails there; the reflex assay covers daratumumab only; and detection limits vary by method and laboratory.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: IFE cannot split drug from IgG κ clone

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “SPEP finds and measures · IFE names and is about 5–10 times more sensitive”, “Before calling a clone: check the tube (fibrinogen, hemolysis) and the drug list (IgG1 kappa antibodies)”.

cues.text: Confirm every suspicious band by immunofixation, and before calling it the patient’s clone rule out fibrinogen from incomplete clotting, hemolysis and a therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibody such as daratumumab.

props.label: SPEP finds + measures · IFE names, ~5–10× more sensitive
Check the tube (fibrinogen, hemolysis) + the drug list

explanation.what: Plain language: a band on an electrophoresis gel is not automatically the patient’s cancer clone. The more sensitive immunofixation test names the band, but drug antibodies, a badly clotted tube or hemolysis can make fake bands, and real small bands can hide among normal proteins. Scientific terms: serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), serum immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE), M-protein, limit of detection, therapeutic monoclonal antibody (t-mAb), daratumumab, isatuximab, elotuzumab, IgG1 kappa, daratumumab IFE reflex assay (DIRA), mass spectrometry, fibrinogen interference, thrombin, hemolysis, transferrin, C3, beta region.
explanation.why: Response categories in myeloma depend on whether the M-protein is still detectable, and complete response requires a negative IFE. A drug band read as disease under-calls response; a pseudo-band read as a paraprotein triggers needless work-up; a hidden band misses disease.
explanation.measure: SPEP limit of detection about 0.5–2 g/L; IFE about 0.1–0.2 g/L (about 5–10 times more sensitive) but not quantitative. Therapeutic antibodies usually circulate below about 2 g/L. Fibrinogen bands sit between beta and gamma; thrombin treatment removes them. Beta-migrating M-proteins are the hardest to quantify.
explanation.differs: SPEP (detect and quantify) vs IFE (type and confirm); patient’s IgG kappa clone vs IgG1 kappa drug band (DIRA shifts daratumumab only); true paraprotein vs fibrinogen or hemolysis pseudo-peak.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a treated patient with a faint IgG kappa band (think drug), a band between beta and gamma in a heparinised or plasma sample (think fibrinogen), or the test that is more sensitive and types the clone (IFE).

comparisons.title: SPEP vs serum IFE
comparisons.distinguisher: Measure the size with SPEP; confirm and type the clone with IFE.

mnemonic.text: Before you call a band a clone, check its ID, the tube and the drug list: IFE gives the ID, the tube tells you if it clotted and is free of hemolysis, and the drug list tells you if a therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibody is on board.
mnemonic.explanation: Three checks that separate a true M-protein from the commonest impostors.
mnemonic.limitation: IFE cannot separate a drug band from an IgG kappa clone of the same isotype; DIRA works only for daratumumab; detection limits vary by method and laboratory.

takeaway: Confirm every suspicious band by immunofixation, and before calling it the patient’s clone rule out fibrinogen from incomplete clotting, hemolysis and a therapeutic IgG1 kappa antibody such as daratumumab.

questions.stem: A patient with IgG kappa myeloma in near-complete response on daratumumab shows a faint IgG kappa band on serum immunofixation. What is the best next laboratory step?

options.text: Perform the daratumumab IFE reflex assay (or mass spectrometry) to separate drug from clone
options.rationale: Correct. Daratumumab is an IgG1 kappa antibody that comigrates with an IgG kappa clone; DIRA shifts the drug band away.
Incorrect. The band may be the drug itself, which mimics residual disease.

options.text: Repeat SPEP, which is more sensitive than IFE
options.rationale: Incorrect. IFE is about 5–10 times more sensitive than SPEP.

options.text: Ignore the band because therapeutic antibodies never appear on IFE
options.rationale: Incorrect. Therapeutic antibodies are whole immunoglobulins and are detected by IFE.

questions.stem: A haemodialysis patient’s serum, drawn through a heparin-locked central catheter, shows a narrow band between the beta and gamma zones. Which explanation should be excluded first?

options.rationale: Correct. Heparin can prevent full clotting; fibrinogen forms a band between beta and gamma that thrombin treatment removes.

options.text: An IgM pentamer that is too large to migrate
options.rationale: Incorrect. This does not explain a pseudo-band linked to heparin and incomplete clotting.
Incorrect. Free light chains are hard to see on serum electrophoresis and are not linked to heparin contamination.
Incorrect. A polyclonal increase is a broad rise, not a narrow band.

questions.stem: Why can a small IgA M-protein be missed on SPEP even though immunofixation detects it?

options.text: It often migrates in the beta region, where transferrin and C3 crowd the trace, and SPEP is less sensitive than IFE
options.rationale: Correct. Beta-migrating M-proteins are the hardest to see and quantify, and IFE detects lower concentrations.
Incorrect. This is not a reason given by the sources.
Incorrect. SPEP detects any monoclonal peak large enough to see, regardless of class.

options.text: IFE cannot detect IgA, so the band must be an artifact
options.rationale: Incorrect. IFE uses anti-IgA antiserum and identifies IgA bands.

claims.text: SPEP detects and quantifies; IFE types heavy and light chain, is about 5–10 times more sensitive, is not quantitative; complete response requires negative IFE.
Daratumumab and isatuximab (anti-CD38) and elotuzumab (anti-SLAMF7) are IgG1 kappa; detected by IFE; usually <2 g/L; mimic residual disease when the clone is the same isotype.
DIRA uses anti-daratumumab to shift the drug band; daratumumab only; mass spectrometry distinguishes several drugs.
Incomplete clotting (residual heparin) leaves fibrinogen, a band between beta and gamma that mimics an M-protein; thrombin removes it.
Hemolysis, elevated CRP and iodinated contrast can create pseudo-M-protein peaks; recollection removed a hemolysis/fibrinogen beta peak in a review example.
IgA M-proteins often migrate in beta, where transferrin and C3 distort the trace; beta-migrating M-proteins are hardest to quantify; IFE confirms clonality.
Reviewer: hemolysis gives a beta-region band near transferrin and a red band visible before staining. Not found in the sources read; not taught.
Reviewer: small bands in the alpha-2 region hide behind C3/other proteins, and bands sitting between normal proteins may be disregarded. Not specifically found in the sources read; not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 47 Hit 13 and Exam Trap 2 name only daratumumab and elotuzumab. Radocha 2021 and Lee 2026 add that isatuximab (IgG1κ) also interferes, that the drug band (usually <2 g/L) matters mainly near VGPR/CR and when the patient’s own clone is IgG kappa, and that DIRA resolves daratumumab only, with mass spectrometry for other drugs (register flag rv-tmab-mspike-context).

Ch. 47 Hit 14 and Exam Trap 3 list fibrinogen and hemolysis, place the hemolysis band near transferrin and say a red band is visible before staining. Lee 2026 and Pires 2025 add elevated CRP, iodinated contrast and antibiotics as pseudo-peak causes, and Rade 2020 locates the fibrinogen band between beta and gamma (residual heparin, removable with thrombin); the transferrin location and the red-band sign were not found in the sources read and are not taught (register flag rv-spep-pseudo-band-causes).
